body.input: do you think we would be able to find a common language?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Well, by the time we're saying aliens are visiting us, we've already prejudiced the whole story

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: because the concept of an alien actually visiting, so to speak, we already know they're kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: things that make sense to talk about visiting. So we already know they exist in the same kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: of physical setup that we do. They're not, it's not just radio signals. It's an actual

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: thing that shows up and so on. So I think in terms of, can one find ways to communicate?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Well, the best example we have of this right now is AI. I mean, that's our first sort of example

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: of alien intelligence. And the question is, how well do we communicate with AI? If you were to say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: if you were in the middle of a neural net and you open it up and it's like, what are you thinking?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Can you discuss things with it? It's not easy, but it's not absolutely impossible. So I think,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: I think by the time, but given the setup of your question, aliens visiting, I think the answer is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: yes, one will be able to find some form of communication, whatever communication means,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: communication requires notions of purpose and things like this. It's a kind of philosophical

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: quagmire. So if AI is a kind of alien life form, what do you think visiting looks like? So if we

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: look at aliens visiting and we'll get to discuss computation and the world of computation, but

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: if you were to imagine, you said you're already prejudiced something by saying you visit,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: but what, how would aliens visit? By visit, there's kind of an implication. And here we're

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: using the imprecision of human language, you know, in a world of the future. And if that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: represented in computational language, we might be able to take the concept visit and go look in

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: the documentation basically, and find out exactly what does that mean? What properties does it have?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And so on. But by visit in ordinary human language, I'm kind of taking it to be, there's,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: you know, something, a physical embodiment that shows up in a spacecraft since we can't see it

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: craft since we kind of know that that's necessary. We're not imagining it's just, you know, photons

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: showing up in a radio signal that, you know, a photons in some very elaborate pattern, we're

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: imagining it's, it's physical things made of atoms and so on that that show up. Can it be

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: photons in a pattern? Well, that's good question. I mean, whether there is the possibility, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: what counts as intelligence? Good question. I mean, it's, you know, and I used to think there was

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: sort of a, oh, they'll be, you know, it'll be clear what it means to find extraterrestrial

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: intelligence, etc, etc, etc. I've, I've increasingly realized as a result of science that I've done,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: that there really isn't a bright line between the intelligent and the merely computational,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: so to speak. So, you know, in our kind of everyday sort of discussion, we'll say things like, you

body.input: know, the weather has a mind of its own. Well, let's unpack that question. You know, we realize

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Not obvious, that would be the case. I mean, that's a science fact. Well,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: say much about what's outside our universe, because by definition, our universe is what we

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: exist within. Now, can we make a sort of almost theological conclusion from being able to know

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: how our particular universe works? Interesting question. I don't think that if you ask the

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: question, could we, and it relates again to this question about extraterrestrial intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: you know, we've got the rule for the universe. Was it built on purpose? Hard to say. That's the

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: same thing as saying we see a signal from, you know, that we're, you know, receiving from some,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: you know, random star somewhere, and it's a series of pulses. And, you know, it's a periodic

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: series of pulses, let's say. Was that done on purpose? Can we conclude something about the

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: origin of that series of pulses? Just because it's elegant does not necessarily mean that somebody

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: created it or that we can even comprehend what we created. Yeah, I think it's the ultimate version

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: of the sort of identification of the technosignature question. It's the ultimate version of that is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: was our universe a piece of technology, so to speak, and how on earth would we know? Because,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: but I mean, it'll be, it's, I mean, you know, in the kind of crazy science fiction thing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: you could imagine, you could say, oh, somebody's going to have, you know, there's going to be a

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: signature there, it's going to be, you know, made by so and so. But there's no way we could

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: understand that, so to speak, and it's not clear what that would mean. Because the universe simply,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: you know, this, if we find a rule for the universe, we're not, we're simply saying that rule

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: represents what our universe does. We're not saying that that rule is something running on a

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: big computer and making our universe. It's just saying that represents what our universe does in

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: the same sense that, you know, laws of classical mechanics, differential equations, whatever they

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: are, represent what mechanical systems do. It's not that the mechanical systems are somehow running

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: solutions to those differential equations. Those differential equations just representing the

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: behavior of those systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: So what's the gap in your sense to linger on the fascinating, perhaps slightly sci-fi question?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: What's the gap between understanding the fundamental rules that create a universe and

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: engineering a system, actually creating a simulation ourselves? You've talked about, sort of,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: you've talked about, you know, nanoengineering, kind of ideas that are kind of exciting, actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: creating some ideas of computation in the physical space. How hard is it as an engineering problem

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: to create the universe once you know the rules that create it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Well, that's an interesting question. I think the substrate on which the universe is operating

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: is not a substrate that we have access to. I mean, the only substrate we have is that same substrate

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: that the universe is operating in. So if the universe is a bunch of hypergraphs being rewritten,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: then we get to attach ourselves to those same hypergraphs being rewritten. We don't get to –

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: and if you ask the question, you know, is the code clean? You know, can we write nice, elegant

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: code with efficient algorithms and so on? Well, that's an interesting question. That's this

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: question of how much computational reducibility there is in the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: But I've seen some beautiful cellular automata that basically create copies of itself within itself,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: right? So that's the question whether it's possible to create – like whether you need to

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: understand the substrate or whether you can –

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Yeah, well, right. I mean, so one of the things that is sort of one of my slightly sci-fi

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: thoughts about the future, so to speak, is, you know, right now, if you poll typical people,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: you say, do you think it's important to find the fundamental theory of physics? You get – because

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: I've done this poll informally at least – it's curious, actually. You get a decent fraction of

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: people saying, oh, yeah, that would be pretty interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: I think that's becoming, surprisingly enough, more – I mean, there's a lot of people are interested

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: in physics in a way that – like without understanding it, just kind of watching

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: scientists, a very small number of them, struggle to understand the nature of our reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Right. I mean, I think that's somewhat true. And in fact, in this project that I'm launching into

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: to try and find the fundamental theory of physics, I'm going to do it as a very public project. I

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: mean, it's going to be live streamed and all this kind of stuff. I don't know what will happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: It'll be kind of fun. I mean, I think that it's going to be a very interesting project.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: I think that it's the interface to the world of this project. I mean, I figure one feature of this

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: project is, unlike technology projects that basically are what they are, this is a project

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: that might simply fail because it might be the case that it generates all kinds of elegant

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: mathematics that has absolutely nothing to do with the physical universe that we happen to live in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Okay. So we're talking about kind of the quest to find the fundamental theory of physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: The first point is, you know, it's turned out it's kind of hard to find the fundamental theory

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: of physics. People weren't sure that that would be the case. Back in the early days of applying

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: mathematics to science, 1600s and so on, people were like, oh, in a hundred years, we'll know

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: everything there is to know about how the universe works. Turned out to be harder than that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And people got kind of humble at some level because every time we got to sort of a greater

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: level of smallness and studying the universe, it seemed like the math got more complicated

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: and everything got harder. When I was a kid, basically, I started doing particle physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And when I was doing particle physics, I always thought finding the fundamental,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: fundamental theory of physics, that's a kooky business. We'll never be able to do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: But we can operate within these frameworks that we built for doing quantum field theory

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: and general relativity and things like this, and it's all good and we can figure out a lot of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Did you even at that time have a sense that there's something behind that too?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Sure. I just didn't expect that. I thought in some rather, it's actually kind of crazy

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: and thinking back on it because it's kind of like there was this long period in civilization

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: where people thought the ancients had it all figured out and will never figure out anything

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: new. And to some extent, that's the way I felt about physics when I was in the middle of doing

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: it, so to speak, was we've got quantum field theory, it's the foundation of what we're doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And yes, there's probably something underneath this, but we'll sort of never figure it out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: But then I started studying simple programs in the computational universe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: things like cellular automata and so on. And I discovered that they do all kinds of things

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: that were completely at odds with the intuition that I had had. And so after that, after you

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: see this tiny little program that does all this amazingly complicated stuff, then you start

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: feeling a bit more ambitious about physics and saying, maybe we could do this for physics too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And so that got me started years ago now in this kind of idea of could we actually find what's

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: underneath all of these frameworks like quantum field theory and general relativity and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And people perhaps don't realize as clearly as they might that the frameworks we're using for

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: physics, which is basically these two things, quantum field theory, sort of the theory of small

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: stuff and general relativity, theory of gravitation and large stuff, those are the two basic theories,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: and they're 100 years old. I mean, general relativity was 1915, quantum field theory,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: well, 1920s, so basically 100 years old. And it's been a good run. There's a lot of stuff

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: been figured out. But what's interesting is the foundations haven't changed. They're not

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: the same. The foundations haven't changed in all that period of time, even though the foundations

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: had changed several times before that in the 200 years earlier than that. And I think the kinds

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: of things that I'm thinking about, which are sort of really informed by thinking about computation

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: and the computational universe, it's a different foundation. It's a different set of foundations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And might be wrong, but it is at least we have a shot. And I think it's, to me, it's my personal

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: intuition for myself is if it turns out that the finding the fundamental theory of physics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: it's kind of low hanging fruit, so to speak, it'd be a shame if we just didn't think to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: If people just said, oh, you'll never figure that stuff out. And it takes another 200 years before

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: he gets around to doing it. I don't know how low hanging this fruit actually is. It may be that it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: kind of the wrong century to do this project. I think the cautionary tale for me, I think about

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: things that I've tried to do in technology where people thought about doing them a lot earlier.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: My favorite example is probably Leibniz, who thought about making essentially encapsulating

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: the world's knowledge in a computational form in the late 1600s and did a lot of things towards that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And basically, we finally managed to do this, but he was 300 years too early. And that's kind of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: in terms of life planning, it's kind of like avoid things that can't be done in your century,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: so to speak. Yeah, timing is everything. So you think if we kind of figure out the underlying

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: rules it can create from which quantum field theory and general relativity can emerge,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: do you think they'll help us unify it at that level of abstraction?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: We'll know it completely. We'll know how that all fits together, yes, without a question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And I mean, it's already, even the things I've already done, they're very, you know, it's very,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: very elegant, actually, how things seem to be fitting together. Now, you know, is it right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: I don't know yet. It's awfully suggestive. If it isn't right, then the designer of the universe

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: should feel embarrassed, so to speak, because it's a really good way to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And your intuition in terms of designing universe, does God play dice?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Is there randomness in this thing? Or is it deterministic? So the kind of...

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: That's a little bit of a complicated question because when you're dealing with these things

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: that involve these rewrites that have... Okay. Even randomness is an emergent phenomenon,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: perhaps. Yes. I mean, it's a... Yeah. Well, randomness... In many of these systems,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: pseudo-randomness and randomness are hard to distinguish. In this particular case,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: the current idea that we have about measurement in quantum mechanics is something very bizarre and

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: very abstract. And I don't think I can yet explain it without kind of yakking about very technical

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: things. Eventually, I will be able to. But if that's right, it's kind of a weird thing because

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: it slices between determinism and randomness in a weird way that hasn't been sliced before,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: so to speak. So like many of these questions that come up in science, where it's like, is it this

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: or is it that? Turns out the real answer is it's neither of those things. It's something kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: different and sort of orthogonal to those categories. And so that's the current, this

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: week's idea about how that might work. But we'll see how that unfolds. I mean, there's this question

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: about a field like physics and sort of the quest for fundamental theory and so on. And there's both

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: the science of what happens and there's the sort of the social aspect of what happens because

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: in a field that is basically as old as physics, we're at, I don't know what it is, fourth

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: generation, I don't know fifth generation, I don't know what generation it is of physicists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And like I was one of these, so to speak. And for me, the foundations were like the pyramid,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: so to speak. It was that way and it was always that way. It is difficult in an old field

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: to go back to the foundations and think about rewriting them. It's a lot easier in young fields

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: where you're still dealing with the first generation of people who invented the field.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And it tends to be the case that the nature of what happens in science tends to be,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: you'll get typically the pattern is some methodological advance occurs. And then there's

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: a period of five years, 10 years, maybe a little bit longer than that, where there's lots of things

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: that are now made possible by that methodological advance, whether it's, I don't know, telescopes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: or whether that's some mathematical method or something. Something happens, a tool gets built,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: and then you can do a bunch of stuff. And there's a bunch of low-hanging fruit to be picked. And

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: that takes a certain amount of time. After all that low-hanging fruit is picked, then it's a hard

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And so it is inexorable in that case that, you know, if if I'm involved in finding how that rule works, then, you know, then that's a it's inexorable that the universe set it up that way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: But I think, you know, one of the things I find a little bit, you know, this goal of finding fundamental theory of physics, for example, if indeed we end up as the sort of virtualized consciousness,

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: the the disappointing feature is people will probably care less about the fundamental theory of physics in that setting than they would now because, gosh, it's like, you know, what the machine code is down below underneath this thing is much less important if you're virtualized, so to speak.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And I think the although I think my my own personal you talk about ego, I find it just amusing that, you know, kind of, you know, if you if you imagine that sort of virtualized consciousness, like what does the virtualized consciousness do for the rest of eternity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: Well, you can explore, you know, the video game that represents the universe as the universe is, or you can go off, you can go off that reservation and go and start exploring the computational universe of all possible universes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And so in some vision of the future of history, it's like the disembodied consciousnesses are all sort of pursuing things like my new kind of science, sort of for the rest of eternity, so to speak, and that that ends up being the, the kind of the the the thing that represents the, you know, the future of kind of the human condition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: I don't think there's a better way to end it. Stephen, thank you so much. It's a huge honor talking today. Thank you so much.

body.input: This was great. You did very well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: And now let me leave you with some words from Stephen Wolfram.

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

metadata.title: Podcast: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89

body.input: For the principle implies that what goes on inside us can ultimately achieve just the same level of computational sophistication as our whole universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: As a side note, let me say that I was always a fan of strength, both powerlifting and Olympic

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: weightlifting, both as a fan and practitioner.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: Personally I'm a fan of people who are willing to put in years of hard work towards finding

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: out what the limits of their body is and then smashing past those limits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: People like Chris Duffin or on the Olympic weightlifting side, people like Dmitriy Klokov.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: That guy's great.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: This is why I love watching the Olympics, both the hard breaks and the triumphs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: They all reveal the incredible heights that the human mind and the human body can reach.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: This is the Lex Freedman podcast and here is my conversation with Chris Duffin.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: You've been a part of several incredible feats of strength.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: Which was the hardest or maybe one you're most proud of?

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: Definitely the one I'm most proud of is that journey for the grand goals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: It was like a five year scope that I chased this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And so when you think about training, it took more than five years, obviously.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: By that point I'd been training for over 25 years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: But it makes me proud.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: I mean there were three distinct things that I wanted to accomplish out of this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: So it was really thought out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And this was kind of my exit from being a competitive lifter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And basically saying, hey, I'm going to be an Instagram lifter, an exhibition lifter,

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: I've done this for 16 years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: I was number one in the world for like eight years straight, all time world records.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And I'm like, I'm not going to do that anymore.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: What I want to do is just something deep down to me that is really important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And there's three things that were driving this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And this is a five year journey that I went through to do this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: I really wanted to showcase that you could do something that is well beyond the scope

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: of what people think is humanly possible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: So just this inspiration thing, this grand over the top.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: Like if you set your mind to a single minded goal, you can go so much further.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And I didn't even say what the goal was upfront because it was so far out there, I would have

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: been laughed at.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And I think big goals should be kept pretty damn close to start with for that reason too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And then the second piece was to walk the walk, to show the principles of what I believed

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: in around human movement, the ability to manage and control the spinal mechanics and the output

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: that can have on the body.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And so I wanted to take the two most basic movements that every able bodied person should

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: be able to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: So fundamental movement patterns, the squat, which is like in the developmental approach

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: is around nine months as a baby from a developmental kinesiology standpoint and a really basic

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: pattern that every able bodied person should be able to master.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: The other one being the hip hinge, being able to pick something up off the ground, a deadlift.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And I wanted to do those two, not just one, because I wanted to show the principles that

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: I wasn't built for one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: I wasn't a specialist because of my lever links, torso links, all that, any outliers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: Because nobody had ever done a thousand pound squat, so this is it, and a thousand pound

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: deadlift.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: It was outside of the scope of what anybody's, there's like half a dozen people that have

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: done one or the other, but nobody's ever done both.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And I wanted to do something unique.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: I wanted to do them, not only do it, but do them for reps to leave literally no question

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: out there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And there's no competition for that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: So it was, this is what I'm going to go do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And to pull it off, I had some past issues with my elbows and stuff that I couldn't work

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: around.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: So I had to wear straps, which was another reason I couldn't do it in the competition

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: setting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: So the first year I worked up and I did a thousand and two pound deadlift.

body.input: And I did it for almost three reps.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: And that still stands as a Guinness World Record, just the one rep does, as the most

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: weight ever sumo deadlifted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: Bjornsson from Game of Thrones.

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

body.input: So then the next four years, and I did a bunch of feats of strength on the way, but it was

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

metadata.title: Podcast: Chris Duffin: The Mad Scientist of Strength | Lex Fridman Podcast #207

metadata.title: Podcast: Tom Brands: Iowa Wrestling | Lex Fridman Podcast #245

metadata.title: Podcast: Tom Brands: Iowa Wrestling | Lex Fridman Podcast #245

body.input: This is the Lex Friedman Podcast, and here is my conversation with Katherine DeClear.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: Why is Pluto not a planet anymore?

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: Does this upset you or has justice finally been served?

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: I get asked this all the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: I think all planetary scientists get asked about Pluto, especially by kids, which is

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: love for Pluto to still be a planet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: The reality is, when we first discovered Pluto, it was a unique object in the outer solar

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: system and we thought we were adding a planet to the inventory of planets that we had.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: Then over time, it became clear that Pluto was not a unique large object in the outer

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: solar system, that there were actually many of these.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: As we started discovering more and more of them, we realized that the concept of Pluto

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: being a planet didn't make sense unless maybe we added all the rest of them as planets.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: You could have imagined actually a different direction that this could have gone where

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: all the other objects that were discovered in that belt, or at least all the ones, let's

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: say, above a certain size, became planets instead of Pluto being declassified.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: But we're now aware of many objects out there in the outer solar system and what's called

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: the Kuiper belt that are of the same size or in some cases even larger than Pluto.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: The declassification was really just a realization that it was not in the same category as the

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: other planets in the solar system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: We basically needed to refine our definition in such a way that took into account that

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: there's this belt of debris out there in the outer solar system of things with a range

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: of sizes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: Is there a hope for clear categorization of what is a planet and not?

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: Or is it all just gray area?

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: When you study planets, when you study moon satellites of those planets, is there lines

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: that could be cleanly drawn or is it just a giant mess?

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: It's just all like a fluid, let's say not mess, but it's like fluid of what is a planet,

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: what is a moon of a planet, what is debris, what is asteroids, all that kind of...

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: So there are technically clear definitions that were set down by the IAU, the International

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: Astronomy Union.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: Is it size related?

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: What are the parameters based on what?

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: So the parameters are that it has to orbit the sun, which was essentially to rule out

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: satellites.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: Of course, this was a not very forward thinking definition because it technically means that

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: all extra solar planets according to that definition are not planets.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: So it has to orbit the sun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: It has to be large enough that its gravity has caused it to become spherical in shape,

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: which also applies to satellites and also applies to Pluto.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: The third part of the definition is the thing that really rules out everything else, which

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: is that it has to have cleared out its orbital path.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: And because Pluto orbits in a belt of material, it doesn't satisfy that stipulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: Why didn't you clear out the path?

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: It's not big enough to knock everybody out of the way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: And this actually is not the first time that has happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: So Ceres, when it was discovered, Ceres is the largest asteroid in the asteroid belt.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: And it was originally considered a planet when it was first discovered.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: And it went through exactly the same story, history, where people actually realized that

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: it was just one of many asteroids in the asteroid belt region.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: And then it got declassified to an asteroid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: And now it's back to a dwarf planet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: So there is a lot of reclassification.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: So to me, as somebody who studies solar system objects, I just personally don't care.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: My level of interest in something has nothing to do with what it's classified as.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: So my favorite objects in the solar system are all moons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: And frequently when I talk about them, I refer to them as planets because to me they are

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: planets.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: They have volcanoes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: They have geology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: They have atmospheres.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: They're planet-like worlds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: And so the distinction is not super meaningful to me, but it is important just for having

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184

body.input: a general framework for understanding and talking about things to have a precise definition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Katherine de Kleer: Planets, Moons, Asteroids & Life in Our Solar System | Lex Fridman Podcast #184
